tldr: We present "OpenTac," an open ecosystem that automatically designs and manufactures 3D force (normal and shear) tactile skins fitting any robot surface from text or 3D models, offering a one-stop workflow from simulation to ultra-fast sampling exceeding 1 kHz.
hero_caption: Example of tactile data measured with OpenTac. The heatmaps represent normal loads, the cyan arrows show shear vectors for each bump, and the white arcs indicate estimated rotations. It clearly demonstrates that both normal and shear forces are cleanly captured across various geometries, from flat surfaces to gripper fingertips.
overview:
For robots to manipulate objects as dexterously as humans, tactile sensing that captures the feel of contact is indispensable. However, conventional tactile sensors have rigid rectangular shapes or can only measure normal forces, making it extremely difficult to fit them to the curved surfaces of robot hands. Building custom sensors from scratch required specialized expertise across circuit design, routing, mechanical fabrication, and data readout, creating a massive barrier for researchers.

To solve this, the authors conceived a simple yet clever structure: stacking an elastomer layer with raised "bumps" on top of an inexpensive piezoresistive film and a single-layer flexible printed circuit board (FPCB). When a bump tilts sideways, the pressure balance across the underlying electrode group shifts, enabling simultaneous recovery of both shear forces (lateral sliding forces) and normal forces through straightforward differential calculations. Furthermore, they developed "OpenTac-CAD," a compiler that fully automates the generation of manufacturing CAD files from 2D contours, 3D meshes, or even natural language prompts like "make a sensor that fits this robot fingertip."

For validation, they fabricated more than 30 distinct sensor designs and verified their functionality. They comprehensively demonstrated performance through comparisons with commercial sensors, MuJoCo-based physical simulation, and a partial scanning method that intelligently reads only active contact regions at over 1 kHz. As a result, they showed that acquiring shear forces dramatically improves success rates in contact-rich physical manipulation tasks such as peg insertion and key turning. With everything from hardware to software released open source, this work significantly lowers the entry barrier for tactile research.
contributions: Developed a scalable tactile skin structure that accurately estimates both normal and shear forces (3D forces) simultaneously using deformation of elastomeric bumps over low-cost piezoresistive film and single-layer FPCB.
Created "OpenTac-CAD," a compiler that fully automates circuit routing and manufacturing file generation from 2D outlines, developable 3D surfaces, or natural language prompts.
Built an integrated ecosystem around manufacturing metadata (manifests) that incorporates FEM-based physical simulation (OpenTac-Sim) and cross-sensor data transfer (OpenTac-Transfer).
Achieved ultra-fast readout at 1286 Hz on a 1024-taxel tactile array—a 19.2x speedup over conventional raster scanning—via contact-localized adaptive sampling (OpenTac-Xampling).

sections.heading: Toward a World Where Anyone Can Freely Create Robot Touch
sections.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, but existing tactile sensors are constrained by fixed geometries or normal-only force sensing. This work introduces OpenTac, an open ecosystem encompassing 3D-force tactile skins fitting arbitrary geometries along with a full pipeline from design to control and learning.
sections.details:
For robots to operate in dynamic, complex real-world environments, tactile sensing that swiftly detects the moment of contact and early onset of slip is vital. However, the shapes of robot hands and bodies vary widely. Until now, researchers either had to design robots around fixed, commercially available rectangular sensors, or learn circuit and CAD design from scratch to handcraft custom sensors.

Thin, flexible tactile skins represent an ideal approach for covering robot surfaces, yet many prior efforts (such as FlexiTac) only measure 1D normal indentation and require manual redesign whenever shapes change. Magnetic 3D sensors also suffer from rigid PCB layouts and slow sampling rates around 30 to 100 Hz, leaving them unable to capture millisecond-scale impact events.

OpenTac was developed to break down these barriers. By combining inexpensive piezoresistive film, single-layer flexible printed circuit boards (FPCBs), and an elastomeric bump cover, it measures both normal and shear forces at millimeter-scale resolution. Furthermore, by integrating the OpenTac-CAD design tool, the OpenTac-Sim physics simulator, OpenTac-Transfer for cross-sensor data migration, and OpenTac-Xampling for smart contact readout exceeding 1 kHz, it provides an environment where anyone can readily bring tactile sensing to robots.

captions.F1: Diverse contact patterns measured with OpenTac skins. Showing (a) dome and clipper rotations on a 64x64 array, (b) thumb twisting on a 9x9 fingertip sensor, (c) can and ball rolling on a UMI gripper fingertip, and (d) up-and-down screwdriver motions. It visually highlights that local shear vectors (cyan arrows) are accurately retrieved alongside normal loads (heatmaps).

sections.heading: Key Differences from Existing Tactile Hardware and Simulators
sections.summary: While diverse tactile sensors exist—including optical sensors like GelSight, magnetic sensors like uSkin, and stretchable textiles—rarely do they combine customizability, 3D force measurement, and high speed. OpenTac stands apart by automating the entire pipeline from robot CAD geometry to PCB design, simulation, and high-speed readout.
sections.details:
Tactile sensing hardware encompasses various modalities, including optical, magnetic, capacitive, and resistive approaches. Vision-based tactile sensors like GelSight and GelSlim deliver high spatial resolution, but embedded cameras and illumination make fingertips thick and bulky. Conversely, magnetic sensors like ReSkin and AnySkin feature thin, swappable skins, yet their rigid circuit boards cannot freely conform to arbitrary curved robot surfaces.

Among flexible tactile skins, prior works include RobotSweater using stretchable fabrics and FlexiTac using FPCBs. However, many only measure normal pressure and miss shear forces, which are critical for early slip detection during grasping. While using mechanical bumps to convert lateral loads into differential pressure is an established concept, OpenTac innovates by combining this principle with automated single-layer FPCB circuit routing.

On the software and simulation front, platforms like TACTO and DiffTactile were tailored to optical sensors or fixed geometries. In contrast, OpenTac-Sim directly imports auto-generated sensor design metadata (the manifest) to build finite element method (FEM) models automatically, allowing custom sensors of any shape to be simulated immediately in MuJoCo. Moreover, tight integration between hardware and software—such as OpenTac-Transfer for preserving learned policy compatibility and OpenTac-Xampling for adaptive high-speed readout—distinguishes this system from standalone sensor studies.

sections.heading: Four Pillars Supporting Design, Simulation, and Ultra-Fast Readout
sections.summary: OpenTac comprises 3D force hardware and four core pillars: automated design (CAD), physics simulation (Sim), cross-sensor transfer (Transfer), and adaptive high-speed sampling (Xampling). All elements interface seamlessly through a shared specification file known as the "manifest."
sections.details:
### 3.1 OpenTac: Sensor Architecture Decoupling Normal and Shear Forces
The hardware design is remarkably simple, consisting of three stacked layers: a single-layer FPCB on the bottom, a piezoresistive film (e.g., Velostat), and an elastomeric bump cover. Interdigitated electrodes at row-column intersections on the FPCB form individual pressure-sensing taxels. The key innovation is placing one raised bump directly over a small taxel cluster (nominally a $2\times 2$ grid of four taxels). When pressed purely downward, pressure distributes evenly across all four taxels, yielding normal force $h_z$ as a common-mode signal. Conversely, lateral shear forces tilt the bump and induce differential pressure between opposite taxels, enabling calculation of shear forces $h_x, h_y$ via differential responses.

### 3.2 OpenTac-CAD: Automatic Manufacturing File Generation from Geometry
OpenTac-CAD is a compiler that takes 2D boundary outlines or unwrapped 3D robot meshes (developable surfaces) and automatically generates taxel layouts, PCB routing, and connector pin assignments within seconds. Users can configure taxel sizes, pitches, and routing clearances. It performs boundary-conformal routing to route traces along the shortest non-overlapping paths to connectors. Furthermore, through LLM integration (e.g., Claude Opus), it can design circuit boards directly from natural language prompts like "design a sensor that fits an Allegro Hand fingertip." Upon compilation, it outputs production-ready Gerber files alongside a "manifest" file recording physical taxel coordinates and electrical connectivity.

### 3.3 OpenTac-Sim: Physics Simulator Auto-Built from Manifests
Running in MuJoCo, OpenTac-Sim automatically generates a tetrahedral FEM mesh matching the sensor geometry simply by loading the manifest. It simulates bump deformation under contact using linear elasticity FEM, computes contact reaction forces on the substrate, and outputs 3-axis forces matching the physical equations. Integrated with robot arms and grippers, it enables reinforcement learning and imitation learning of contact-rich tasks directly in simulation.

### 3.4 OpenTac-Transfer: Tactile Data Mapping Across Morphologies
Across different robots and sensor resolutions, OpenTac-Transfer aligns contact surfaces using the physical coordinate systems recorded in manifests. It maps normal contact force fields mutually via affine transformation calibration maps, facilitating data reuse without tight coupling to specific sensor hardware.

### 3.5 OpenTac-Xampling: Tracking Active Contacts for >1 kHz Readout
Scanning piezoresistive arrays via conventional raster scanning (reading all elements sequentially from top-left to bottom-right) degrades frame rate proportionally to the element count $N$, missing rapid contact transients under 10 ms. OpenTac-Xampling leverages the spatial locality and temporal continuity of contacts by defining a per-frame sampling budget $M \ll N$. It allocates one quarter of the budget to coarse global exploration and the remaining three quarters to intensely sample regions with recent contact, achieving ultra-high-speed readout under localized contact conditions.

sections.heading: 30+ Fabricated Sensors, Simulation Tests, and Substantial Real-Robot Gains
sections.summary: All 31 auto-generated boards functioned correctly, exhibiting high correlation ($R^2 \ge 0.93$) against commercial reference force sensors. In real-world peg insertion and key turning tasks, adding shear sensing significantly raised success rates, while adaptive sampling enabled ultra-fast detection at 1286 Hz.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Automated Design Validation and LLM Generation
Compiling 31 sensor designs with varied shapes and ordering them through FPCB fabrication services yielded zero design rule check (DRC) violations, and all fabricated boards operated reliably. Compared to standard rectangular grids, conformal packing improved active sensing area coverage on tapered fingertip geometries (e.g., YUBI) from 57% to 75%—an 18-point gain. Compilation took only 0.7 to 2.6 seconds. In experiments prompting an LLM agent with requests like "for a Unitree G1 foot sole" or "gecko silhouette shape," it autonomously produced fully manufacturable CAD data within a median time of 6.5 minutes.

### 4.2 Material Characterization and 3D Force Accuracy
Load-cell characterization evaluated film types (Velostat variants), electrode spacing, and pitch. Chibitronics film offered high sensitivity under light loads but saturated rapidly, whereas LINQSTAT maintained a wide dynamic range up to 60 N without saturating. Benchmarking the standard configuration (LINQSTAT, 4.0 mm pitch, 0.2 mm electrode gap) against a commercial 6-axis reference sensor (OptoForce) demonstrated coefficients of determination ($R^2$) of 0.95 for $F_x$, 0.93 for $F_y$, and 0.96 for $F_z$, with root mean square errors (RMSE) of 0.11 to 0.16 N, confirming high 3D force estimation accuracy.

### 4.3 Impact of Shear Sensing in Real-World Manipulation Learning
Tactile observations were integrated into imitation learning (Action Chunking Transformer: ACT) on a single SO-101 arm and a bimanual YAM robot. In a peg insertion task, proprioception-only (Pose) achieved a 66% success rate and normal-force-only (1D) reached 60%, whereas OpenTac-3D with shear sensing jumped to 82%. In a fine-tolerance plug insertion task where normal pressure alone cannot distinguish surface pressing from socket entry, OpenTac-3D achieved 70% success (versus 54% for Pose and no gain for 1D) by detecting shear transitions. In bimanual key insertion and turning, OpenTac-3D achieved 62% success, substantially outperforming Pose (18%) and 1D (43%).

### 4.4 Ultra-Fast Adaptive Sampling and Durability
On a $32\times 32$ (1024-taxel) skin, OpenTac-Xampling with a sampling budget of $M=16$ boosted readout speed from 67 Hz (conventional raster scanning) to 1286 Hz (a 19.2x increase). In dynamic drop tests where a tennis ball fell from 30 cm (producing ~3 ms transient contact), raster scanning detected the impact in only 2 of 6 trials, whereas adaptive sampling captured the impact across multiple frames in every trial. In 10-hour continuous robot indentation tests on a single bump, an initial drift occurred over the first two hours before stabilizing, maintaining accurate differential separation of relative load changes throughout.

sections.heading: Shaping the Future of Robotics with an Accessible Tactile Ecosystem
sections.summary: OpenTac provides a vertically integrated open ecosystem spanning design, manufacturing, simulation, and high-speed execution. Despite trade-offs like FPCB non-stretchability and piezoresistive hysteresis, releasing the entire hardware and software stack open source provides a valuable catalyst for tactile robotics research.
sections.details:
This work introduced OpenTac, a tactile skin and ecosystem that conforms to custom robot surfaces while measuring full 3D normal and shear forces. By integrating automated CAD generation, FEM simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and high-speed sampling, it substantially lowers barriers to tactile integration.

The paper also discusses several limitations. Standard FPCBs lack stretchability, meaning they cannot conform without darting cuts to doubly curved surfaces like spheres (restricted to developable surfaces). Additionally, using inexpensive piezoresistive films incurs material hysteresis and thermal drift. The adaptive sampling approach also drops to standard raster rates when large-scale, whole-surface contacts occur simultaneously.

Nonetheless, the demonstration across 30+ fabricated sensors, notable manipulation performance gains, and >1 kHz sampling make OpenTac compelling. All hardware schematics, firmware, and simulation code are open-sourced under permissive licenses (opentac.github.io), offering a practical platform for the robotics and embodied AI communities.

takeaways: Leveraging localized differential pressure across elastomeric bumps enables accurate 3D force (normal and shear) sensing using low-cost single-layer piezoresistive film and FPCBs.
In contact-rich tasks like peg insertion and key turning, shear force feedback significantly boosts imitation learning policy success over normal-only sensing.
Decoupling physical geometry from electrical layout via a "manifest" file enables automated pipelines connecting CAD compilation, FEM simulation, and cross-sensor transfer.
Adaptive quadtree sampling exploiting spatial contact locality and temporal continuity sustains >1 kHz readout speeds regardless of expanding array dimensions.
limitations: Standard flexible FPCBs lack stretchability, preventing direct conformal application to doubly curved surfaces like spheres without cuts (limited to developable surfaces).
Piezoresistive films suffer from inherent hysteresis, creep, and thermal drift, recommending periodic recalibration or relative force interpretations for long-duration absolute sensing.
Adaptive sampling (Xampling) relies on localized contact assumptions; wide-area simultaneous contact forces frame rates back down to standard full-grid raster scanning speeds.
